title: 2026-03-30 - POC scoping: benchmark harness integration
next_steps: Samira to share benchmark harness repo + runbook (link) and sample config
Customer to provide representative sample dataset and 1-week traffic profile
Schedule two-hour load test window with SRE (preferred Apr 6-8)
Diego to prepare streaming vs non-streaming test cases and expected metrics
action_items: Samira Patel: Send benchmark harness repo + runbook : 2026-04-02
Ravi Singh: Provide sample prompts + average sequence lengths : 2026-04-03

summary: POC scoping focused on integrating Stratus's inference scripts with Redwood's benchmark harness. Agreed success criteria (latency p95/p99, throughput, cost target), workload sizing (RPS, concurrency, seq lengths), and test plan (streaming vs non-streaming). Next steps include sharing harness, sample data, and scheduling load tests.
transcript: [00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for 45 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:12] Maya (Stratus CTO): Maya here - CTO at Stratus. Ravi, Lena, and Alex are with me. We're trying to validate latency and cost for our summarization endpoint.
[00:24] Ravi (ML Eng): Hi, yeah - main goal is to see production tail latency and p99 under concurrent load. We also care about streaming because customers want progressive chunks.
[00:38] Samira: Great. I'll hand off to Diego to walk through the harness and how we plug in customer scripts.

[00:45] Diego (Redwood SE): thanks. So at a high level our benchmark harness runs customer inference scripts against a test bed - you can run on hosted Redwood infra or dedicated nodes. We support streaming tests (chunked token emit) and non-streaming. For integration we just need a small runner script that calls your model with the same payloads you use in prod.
[01:05] Alex (SRE): For the test runners, do you need VPN/VPC peering? We can't open everything to the internet.

[01:12] Diego: We can run in two modes: 1) our hosted runner that hits your private endpoint over a peered VPC, or 2) we run inside your VPC with a short-lived agent. We'll need a firewall rule for the test IPs or temporary SSH jump, and an IAM role to pull secrets. We'll add that to the runbook.
[01:40] Lena (Infra): That sounds fine. We'll need a checklist for required ports and KMS access. Also SOC2 questions - we'll want to run the harness without sending logs to external buckets.
[01:55] Samira: Understood, we'll include a security appendix - options for no external logs, artifacts kept on-prem, and KMS wrappers. Diego, can you note those?
[02:05] Diego: Yep - note added. On the workload side: tell us RPS targets and typical sequence lengths. That drives batch sizes and KV cache behaviour.

[02:18] Ravi: Our production mix is roughly 40% short queries (avg 32 tokens), 50% medium (avg 256 tokens), 10% long (avg 1,024 tokens). Peak concurrent users ~1200, sustained RPS ~400, bursts to 900 for 2-3 minutes.

[02:40] Diego: Good, that distribution helps. For batching, we'll test with batch sizes 1, 8, 16 and concurrent client threads tuned to match your RPS. For streaming tests we'll simulate chunked token intervals like you expect in the UI.

[02:55] Maya: Our SLA target is p95 < 250ms for short queries and p95 < 800ms for medium; p99 we'd like under 1.5s if possible. Cost target is roughly $0.0008 per short request equivalent - rough number, depends on batching.

[03:18] Diego: We'll map those into measurable success criteria. For the POC we usually define pass/fail as: p95 and p99 thresholds, 99.9% availability during the test window, and unit cost estimates based on observed tokens/sec and infrastructure used.
[03:35] Samira: Timeline-wise, can we aim to run the first baseline tests in the week of April 6? That gives time to exchange artifacts.
[03:45] Maya: Works for us - we need internal calendar confirmation but it's doable.

[04:00] Diego: On harness integration: preferred approach is you hand over a small wrapper script with a function call like infer(payload) that returns either streaming events or final payload. We provide a shim so your code runs inside the harness unchanged.
[04:18] Ravi: Our current client library does streaming over websockets; do you support websocket-based streaming in the harness?

[04:28] Diego: We support websockets and server-sent events. If you can provide a lightweight adapter that exposes the same call pattern, we can plug it in. Otherwise we'll emulate streaming by slicing responses client-side which is less accurate for kernel-level latency but still useful.

[04:50] Alex: Important: we want to measure end-to-end latency including our ingress LB, authentication, and any pre/post-processing layers - not just model inference. Can the harness include those hops?

[05:02] Diego: Yes, you can give us the full endpoint and we'll run through your environment. That increases test complexity (and potential flakiness), but we can do a controlled run window with warm-up and health checks.
[05:18] Samira: Let's capture success criteria explicitly now so we don't misalign. Ravi/Maya: repeat the three metrics you care about.
[05:28] Ravi: 1) p95 for short <250ms; 2) p95 for medium <800ms; 3) p99 for all less than 1.5s. Also throughput: sustain 400 RPS with p95 targets met.
[05:45] Maya: Add cost estimate target per 1k short-equivalent requests - like I said earlier, ballpark $0.8 per thousand requests.

[05:55] Diego: We'll output raw metrics (p50/p95/p99), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, queue times, batching stats, and cost estimate based on observed GPU-hours and our unit pricing model. For streaming we'll measure first-byte latency and time-to-final.
[06:15] Lena: How do you handle caching, specifically KV/prefix caching? We use a lot of repeated prompts with slight edits.

[06:24] Diego: Harness will exercise both cold and warm cache scenarios. We'll run cold-start runs and warm runs after a warm-up phase to measure steady-state behaviour. We'll surface cache hit rates and delta in latency.
[06:40] Samira: On hardware: do you have a preference? We can run on H100s or A100s, or lower-cost T4s for latency-insensitive workloads. Which do you want to test?
[06:52] Maya: Ideally H100 for production parity, but we also want to understand cost on A100 and quantized 4-bit variants.

[07:02] Diego: We'll include three axes: (1) H100 baseline, (2) A100 comparison, (3) quantized variant (8-bit/4-bit) on A100. For each we'll run the same workload and produce unit cost and latency tradeoff charts.
[07:18] Ravi: For quantized models, quality regressions matter. We'll need an eval set to check output quality difference - BLEU/ROUGE or a small human check set.
[07:28] Diego: Yep - include a quality evaluation step. If quality drops beyond your threshold we'll mark quantized config as not acceptable.
[07:38] Maya: Good. Now on test orchestration: how do you control concurrency? We want to model bursts (900 RPS for ~2 minutes).

[07:48] Diego: The harness supports traffic profiles: steady-state, step-burst, and poisson arrival. We'll run a warm-up 10m, then steady 400 RPS for 15m, then burst 900 RPS for 3m, monitor p99 and drop rates.
[08:05] Alex: Are retries counted in the metrics? We have a client-side retry layer; we need to ensure retries don't mask latency issues.
[08:13] Diego: We'll report raw latencies including retries as separate traces and deduplicate requests so you can see application-level RPS vs backend RPS.

[08:25] Samira: A common question: streaming vs non-streaming cost delta - streaming can increase CPU overhead but improve perceived latency. We'll include both tests and show tokens/sec and CPU/GPU utilization.
[08:38] Ravi: For streaming test cases, we need control over chunk sizes and inter-chunk delay to emulate our UI. We'll provide those parameters.
[08:46] Diego: Perfect. Please add chunk-size and average inter-chunk interval to the sample config you send.
[09:00] Maya: On security again: we can't ship PII to external buckets. For artifacts, we prefer host-side collection or a secure S3 in our account with restricted access.
[09:10] Samira: We'll support both options. We'll include an S3-in-customer-account approach in the runbook and provide Terraform snippets for a temporary test bucket with short-lived creds.
[09:24] Lena: Also need audit logs for every test run - who triggered, what config, and PR numbers. That's part of compliance for us.
[09:33] Diego: We'll attach a run metadata file and optional signed logs. We'll include that in the run artifact package.
[09:44] Maya: How long will a single configuration test take end-to-end? We have many permutations (H100/A100/quantized/streaming).

[09:54] Diego: One config (warmup + steady + burst + metrics) typically 30-45 minutes. If we parallelize across hardware it's faster but requires capacity. For the POC we'll probably do sequential runs: baseline on H100, then A100, then quantized; each ~45m, so plan 3-4 hours total in a single day.
[10:12] Ravi: Can you estimate cost for that run? We need to budget for external GPU time if using Redwood-hosted H100s.
[10:19] Samira: We'll provide a cost estimate in the runbook - usually a few hundred to low thousands depending on hardware and run duration; we'll share a preliminary estimate with the repo.

[10:30] Diego: Regarding instrumentation: please expose endpoints for Prometheus metrics if possible; otherwise we'll rely on exported logs. GPU util, queue depth, batch sizes, and latency histograms are key.
[10:45] Alex: We can expose metrics over a read-only endpoint for the test window. We'll send the endpoint and token.
[10:52] Samira: Great. Any blockers on your side to start integration?
[11:00] Maya: Mainly internal approvals and security review to allow Redwood test runners. We'll start that immediately.
[11:08] Lena: Also need the runbook and exact IP ranges and required inbound rules so we can schedule change window with our network team.
[11:18] Samira: We'll include IP ranges and a minimal firewall checklist in the runbook. Diego will attach a sample terraform snippet.
[11:28] Diego: I'll also provide the harness repo link here in chat after call and a sample adapter template for websocket streaming.
[11:36] Maya: One more question: how do you calculate the unit cost per request? Is it GPU-hours amortized over tokens or a different model?

[11:44] Diego: We estimate cost two ways: (1) infra cost: GPU-hours * hourly rate / total served tokens, and (2) Redwood list pricing per token which we use for commercial quoting. We'll show both so you can map to internal cost centers.
[11:58] Ravi: For the quality check during quantized runs, what's the throughput for the eval suite? We want it to run quickly so it doesn't add hours.
[12:08] Diego: Eval suites are typically fast; a few hundred prompts runs in 5-10 minutes on batch. We'll parallelize the eval across replicas to keep wall-clock low.
[12:20] Samira: Ok, we're at 35 minutes - let's do a quick recap and confirm next steps.

[12:28] Samira: Recap: Samira will share harness repo+runbook, Diego prepares baseline configs and streaming adapters, Stratus provides sample prompts, metrics endpoints, and confirms test window. Tentative test week Apr 6. Action items captured in CRM.
[12:45] Maya: Sounds good. Please also include a summary of expected data retention policies during the test run.
[12:52] Samira: Will do. Any final questions?
[13:00] Alex: No, thanks. Looking forward to the repo.
[13:05] Ravi: Thanks everyone. We'll try to get the sample data to you by Apr 3.
[13:12] Samira: Thanks all - we'll follow up with the repo link and calendar invite for the test window. Bye.
[13:18] (call ends)
